title: Perfect $(s,r)$-state transfer
authors: Stephen Kirkland, Hermie Monterde, Sarah Plosker
abstract: Much work has been done in the last two decades on the topic of quantum state transfer in a quantum spin network. One can model such a system of interacting qubits using an undirected graph, and studying vertex-to-vertex dynamics. This setup has recently been relaxed to allow for dynamics between linear combinations of two vertex states, i.e.\ from $\mathbf u = \mathbf e_a + s \mathbf e_b$ to $\mathbf μ=\mathbf e_α + r \mathbf e_β$, where $r=s$ is either $-1$ (which corresponds to pair state transfer) or $+1$ (which corresponds to plus state transfer), or more recently $r=s$ is taken to be any real number (which corresponds to $s$-pair state transfer).   Here, we broaden the investigation of $s$-pair state transfer to \textit{perfect $(s,r)$-state transfer}, which is perfect state transfer from $\mathbf u = \mathbf e_a + s \mathbf e_b$ to $\mathbf μ=\mathbf e_α + r \mathbf e_β$ (up to some dilation) where $r,s\in \mathbb C$. We identify infinite families of graphs with perfect $(s,r)$-state transfer and provide characterizations of cases when $|r|= |s|$ and when $|r|\neq |s|$, showing situations when the degree of entanglement between vertex states is preserved, and when it is not preserved. The latter is particularly important as it represents perfect state transfer from an entangled pair of qubits to another one where the degree of entanglement need not be the same\mdash in fact, it can be set up so as to ``boost'' (increase) entanglement. We provide an algorithm that finds the vector with two nonzero entries that maximizes the fidelity of transfer for a fixed time $t$ starting from a given $s$-pair state $\mathbf u$. Finally, we provide a sensitivity analysis, with respect to readout time errors, of perfect $(s,r)$-state transfer.
summary: This work generalizes quantum state transfer to entangled 's-pair' states on graph structures. It characterizes the conditions for perfect transfer, showing that the entanglement degree can be manipulated, even increased, during the process. The paper also provides tools to analyze the robustness of this transfer against time measurement errors.
main_problem: The paper investigates perfect $(s,r)$-state transfer, which is a generalization of quantum state transfer from an $s$-pair entangled state to an $r$-pair entangled state.
main_result:
The authors identify infinite families of graphs exhibiting this perfect transfer and demonstrate that the degree of entanglement can be boosted (increased) if $|r| 
eq |s|$.
method: The study uses spectral analysis of the transition operator derived from graph Hamiltonians, along with developing algorithms to maximize transfer fidelity and performing sensitivity analysis.
model_or_system: The system is modeled as quantum state transfer on an undirected graph, where the dynamics are governed by a continuous-time quantum walk Hamiltonian (e.g., adjacency or Laplacian matrix). The states are generalized to $s$-pair states, $\mathbf u = \mathbf e_a + s \mathbf e_b$.
key_observables: Fidelity of transfer, degree of entanglement ($|s|$ or $|r|$), and the second derivative of the fidelity function (sensitivity to time errors).
important_parameters: The complex parameters $r$ and $s$ defining the initial and final entangled states, and the graph structure itself.
main_assumptions: The analysis often focuses on the single excitation subspace of the Hamiltonian, and specific results are derived assuming the initial and final states have exactly two non-zero entries.
figures_summary: The notes do not describe specific figures, but mention examples like P5, $K_{1,n}$, and $CP(n)$ used to calculate fidelity and sensitivity.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the generalized PST problem, characterizing it for specific graph families ($K_n, K_{a,b}$), developing algorithms for fidelity maximization, and concluding with sensitivity analysis.
why_interesting: The concept of controlling entanglement transfer and quantifying the robustness of these quantum processes against measurement errors (sensitivity analysis) is highly relevant to designing robust quantum communication protocols.
